summary: Madar  is an English web museum of the hardware NASA and its partners left behind on the Moon, on Mars, in Earth orbit and in deep space, made for school-age space fans. It turns 40 machines, from the Apollo 11 lunar module "Eagle" to Opportunity, Ingenuity and Voyager 1, into archive files. Each file has the real NASA 3D model, its launch date, where it is now, an honest status (Retired, Still working, Still traveling, Active mission or Returned to Earth) and a short story of why it is not forgotten. Visitors explore an atlas of destinations, a launch ledger from 1958 to today and a quiz, and can watch a short narrated film. Most people know the missions, not the machines that stayed out there. Madar gives every machine a voice, and shows young people that the next piece in the museum could be theirs.
details:
What it does: Madar is a free web museum with no accounts. An Atlas lets visitors filter 40 machines by destination, type and status; a Launch Ledger lists every launch date (UTC) from 1958; a quiz tests visitors with real model images; and every machine has a file with its NASA 3D model, location today, status, story and an NSSDCA source link. Partner-agency hardware (Mir, Rosetta, Canadarm) is clearly labelled.

Why it matters: The stories of this hardware are locked in technical archives. Madar presents them as short human stories that inspire students and connect them to NASA's legacy.

How we built it: A fast web app (Vite, JavaScript, Firebase Hosting) with WebGL 3D models from NASA 3D Resources and mission data from the NSSDCA Master Catalog. Our narrated films were composed in Python and FFmpeg from real NASA photographs, with English subtitles.

Team (equal members): Tamim Ali Asiri, Taim Ali Asiri, Tamim Mubarak Al-Qahtani, Turki Majed Dajam, Ayed Al-Qahtani, Saud Saleh Asiri.

AI disclosure: The narration voice in our films was generated with ElevenLabs, and the videos carry a visible "AI-assisted" watermark. Parts of the code and the films were made with assistance from Claude (Anthropic). All photographs and 3D models are authentic NASA resources; no images were AI-generated.
